title: Always Already Using AI: There's No Such Thing as an AI-Free Student Work
author: Stefan Bauschard
summary: Stefan Bauschard challenges the assumption behind school AI policies, namely that a student receives an assignment, decides whether to use AI and chooses how much help to accept. He argues the assumption fails twice: deliberate use is harder to regulate than policies imagine because the system supplies the menu of options and small delegations accumulate, and much of AI's influence never passes through a decision to use it. Drawing on Dewey and Heidegger, he says students are always already using AI, since it shapes what they want to think about, how they write after reading machine-generated prose, and how they expect conversations to go. He cites studies on co-writing and persuasion, structural priming, AI detectors and homogenization to show convergence is the new risk. He argues the blue-book exam interrupts access but not influence, and proposes a standard of accountability: however a sentence was produced, the student must be able to defend it, using tools such as oral defenses and dialogue portfolios.
points: Traffic-light and AI Assessment Scale policies assume a student standing outside AI and choosing to step in, which misses the system's role in framing options and shaping interests.
Small delegations such as explaining, outlining, improving and evaluating add up to a transfer of intellectual work even though each request seems reasonable.
Because writers absorb the patterns of what they read, student prose is likely to drift toward AI patterns, which also explains why detectors can flag work that was honestly written.
The social-dilemma finding that AI lifts each writer while making the group more alike means individual self-regulation cannot fix convergence.
Bauschard proposes a standard of defensibility, with oral defenses, dialogue portfolios and comparison of first and later positions, instead of tracing influence or relying on the blue book.
quotes: A student can write every word themselves and still carry a system’s framing, language, and assumptions into the work without noticing.
The student made a meaningful choice, but the system determined the options. An argument it never proposed may never enter consideration.
The student never decides, “I want AI to do my thinking.” They simply accept the next useful offer.
Willpower is only part of the story. Self-regulation happens inside an environment of defaults, incentives, and social pressure.
A detector, like a teacher squinting at a suspiciously tidy paragraph, tries to read use off the page. The page records influence.
AI can lift each student’s work and still compress the variety across students.
The blue book interrupts access to AI. It does not undo how AI has shaped the student.
The workable standard is simpler and older: however a sentence was produced, it belongs to the student who submits it, and the student has to be able to defend it.
